title: RESCUE: An end-to-end multi-agent LLM system for proactive rare-disease patient screening in the EHR
authors: Liu, C.; Geltzeiler, A.; Afyouni, A.; Nie, M.; Ravi, K.; French, C.; Chung, W.; Wojcik, M. H.
abstract: Rare diseases affect a significant portion of the global population, yet patients often endure a lengthy diagnostic odyssey and miss timely diagnosis with exome or genome sequencing (ES/GS). Existing informatics tools often rely on pre-identified patients or institution-specific rule sets that are laborious to implement locally and rarely address clinical utility and operational feasibility. We introduce RESCUE, an end-to-end, multi-agent LLM-powered workflow that automates the local implementation of both rule-based and machine learning screening algorithms across the entire electronic health record (EHR). Four specialized agents operate in sequence: the Ontology Agent classifies clinical data into a four-tier genetic-evidence taxonomy; the Modeling Agent builds a positive-unlabeled (PU) XGBoost classifier; the Screening Agent applies the model across the EHR and flags patients with a rule-based algorithm; and the Review Agent samples clinical notes to assess medical necessity and operational feasibility. In a retrospective evaluation at a pediatric hospital, the model showed strong discrimination on a holdout set (n=12,591; AUC 0.808). Of 175,842 patients meeting screening criteria, those flagged by RESCUE were 7.4-fold more likely to receive subsequent genomic assessments than controls. Blinded chart review of this group confirmed previously missed, medically appropriate candidates for ES/GS with 80% precision, accounting for prior testing. By decoupling expert roles into modular agents, RESCUE offers a flexible, scalable framework, with machine-learning and rule-based approaches complementing rather than substituting for each other. It also provides a reproducible, agentic pathway for direct local implementation to reduce diagnostic delays on an institutional scale.

infographic.key_insight: RESCUE uses four specialized LLM agents to implement complementary machine-learning and rule-based EHR screening for potentially missed rare-disease testing candidates.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The workflow could help identify patients who may warrant evaluation for exome or genome sequencing, but it does not establish a diagnosis.
method: Ontology Agent organizes clinical data into a four-tier genetic-evidence taxonomy.
Modeling Agent trains a positive-unlabeled XGBoost classifier; Screening Agent applies model-based and rule-based screening.
Review Agent samples clinical notes to assess medical necessity and operational feasibility.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a retrospective pediatric-hospital evaluation, holdout AUC was 0.808 (n=12,591); among 175,842 screening-eligible patients, flagged patients were 7.4-fold more likely than controls to receive subsequent genomic assessments, and blinded chart review found 80% precision for appropriate ES/GS candidacy after accounting for prior testing.
infographic.watch_item: Single-hospital retrospective findings require prospective, external validation before assuming broader clinical benefit or operational feasibility.
infographic.paper_title: RESCUE: An end-to-end multi-agent LLM system for proactive rare-disease patient screening in the EHR

title: BenchmarkHub: an open-source platform for reproducible evaluation of large language models in healthcare
authors: Alvarez-Arenas, J. I.; Jimenez-Carretero, D.; Sanchez-Cabo, F.
abstract: BackgroundLarge language models (LLMs) are solely judged by their scores on biomedical benchmarks, yet these scores are rarely reproducible since the prompts, inference settings and model builds are seldom reported. We developed BenchmarkHub, an open-source platform for auditable evaluation of language and vision-language models for biomedical research. MethodsBenchmarkHub is a Python web application (Django 5.2, SQLite) released under the MIT licence and available at https://github.com/juanjuanignacio/benchmarkhub. The application can be accessed through a browser interface, a set of command-line tools and a REST API, so interactive exploration and scripted pipelines produce identical, comparable records. The platform samples questions with fixed seeds, runs models directly or as tool-using agents in a code sandbox, grades answers with deterministic rules and stores every prompt, reply and tool call. The interface provides a leaderboard to rank performance of the models, allowing model comparison without any preexisting programming knowledge. FindingsWe used BenchmarkHub to evaluate 12 open-weight models in five experiments on 15 biomedical benchmarks (11 text, two multimodal and two computational biology) and two general benchmarks. The pooled accuracy ranged from 46{middle dot}1% (95% CI 43{middle dot}0-49{middle dot}3) to 80{middle dot}9% (78{middle dot}3-83{middle dot}3). Re-grading the responses with simple answer-extraction rules lowered a models accuracy by up to 33{middle dot}1 percentage points leading to a reorder of the leaderboard. Published scores were found for 23 out of the 143 benchmark/model combinations tested. The accuracy measured by BenchmarkHub was lower than in the published results in 19 out of the 23 available comparisons. The effect of four prompting protocols (1: default prompt; 2: asking the model to answer the letter only; 3: extended reasoning; 4: three-shot prompting) changed MEDQA accuracy by up to 11{middle dot}3 points but was not significant after multiple-testing correction with 150 questions. We also tested the impact of ablation on benchmarking using the MMMU benchmark dataset. Removing images lowered the accuracy by 18{middle dot}0 and 19{middle dot}3 points repectively for the two strongest models. Finally, the accuracy of agentic benchmarks using a sandboxed interpreter increased on computational biology tasks by 36-63 points. InterpretationBenchmarking is essential to assess the impact and validity of LLMs for medical applications. BenchmarkHub allows a fair and rigorous comparison of models across established datasets, including the possibility to upload own datasets. The suite includes visual tools to ease model comparison and ranking without any programming knowledge. Self-hosted infrastructure that records every choice and parameter makes benchmark claims checkable without data leaving the institution. FundingEuropean Union EU4Health Programme (JACARDI), Spanish Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities-State Research Agency (MCIN/AEI) with FEDER funds, the European Union Recovery and Resilience Facility-NextGenerationEU, and the Instituto de Salud Carlos III. Research in context Evidence before this studyWe searched PubMed, arXiv and Crossref in October, 2026, for articles published from January, 2022, to October, 2026, without language restrictions, using combinations of the terms "large language model", "benchmark", "evaluation", "reproducibility", "prompt sensitivity", "medical", "clinical", "multimodal", "image", "agent" and "bioinformatics". A systematic review of 519 studies found that LLM evaluations in healthcare rely mainly on exam-style questions, rarely use real patient data and seldom report evaluation settings. Holistic frameworks and new task-specific benchmarks, including two published in this journal have broadened what is measured, but headline scores are usually produced by model developers with incompletely described protocols. Studies outside medicine show that prompt format, answer extraction and nominally deterministic decoding can each change benchmark accuracy substantially, and that many questions in general multimodal benchmarks can be answered from the text alone, without looking at the image. Much of this evidence comes from preprints or developer-run evaluations, and we found no medical study that quantified, on the same items and within one framework, the effects of prompting protocol, answer extraction, image availability and tool access, nor an open, self-hosted platform built for that purpose. Added value of this studyBenchmarkHub is, to our knowledge, the first open-source platform that combines a web interface, command-line and REST access, local and cloud model providers, a sandboxed tool-use agent loop, procedurally generated computational biology benchmarks and a complete per-question audit trail. Using only the platform and 12 locally served open-weight models, we show that the answer-extraction rule alone can change medical accuracy by more than the gaps between models and reorder them, that published scores are usually higher than those measured under a documented protocol, that protocol effects need larger samples than are typically used, that on a medical multimodal benchmark the strongest models kept about 90% of their accuracy without the images, and that tool access transforms performance on computational biology tasks. Implications of all the available evidenceMedical benchmark scores should be reported together with the protocol, answer-extraction rules, decoding settings, model build and input modality that produced them, and comparisons between models should be paired and made under identical conditions. Self-hosted evaluation infrastructure allows hospitals and research institutes to do this for their own candidate models without sharing data, as a reproducible screening step that precedes, and does not replace, clinical validation.

infographic.key_insight: BenchmarkHub makes biomedical LLM evaluations auditable, showing that answer-grading rules alone can shift accuracy by up to 33.1 percentage points and reorder leaderboards.
infographic.clinical_relevance: More transparent benchmarking can support scrutiny of healthcare AI claims, but benchmark performance does not establish clinical safety or effectiveness.
method: Open-source platform with browser, command-line and REST API access.
Fixed-seed sampling, deterministic grading and logging of prompts, replies and tool calls.
Evaluated 12 open-weight models across 15 biomedical and two general benchmarks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Pooled accuracy ranged from 46.1% to 80.9%; BenchmarkHub scores were lower than published results in 19 of 23 available comparisons.
infographic.watch_item: Prompting effects on MEDQA were not significant after multiple-testing correction with 150 questions, limiting conclusions about prompt superiority.
infographic.paper_title: BenchmarkHub: an open-source platform for reproducible evaluation of large language models in healthcare

title: Systematic Benchmarking and Optimization of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for Clinical Phenotyping: A Type II Diabetes Case Study in an ICD-Screened Cohort
authors: Park, H.; Rees, M.; Kruger, N.; Fuse, K.; Castro, V. M.; Gainer, V.; Wattanasin, N.; Benoit, B.; Wagholikar, K. B.; Murphy, S.
abstract: Traditional EHR phenotyping methods can require substantial disease-specific development and long-term maintenance. While integrating large language models (LLMs) with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is promising, the impact of RAG configurations remains underexplored. We systematically evaluated these design choices for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) phenotyping in an ICD-screened cohort. Using GPT-4o, we processed 170,678 clinical notes from 275 patients. We evaluated seven embedding models and three prompt strategies (baseline, improved zero-shot, and few-shot). Using the improved zero-shot prompt, we tested 350 embedding model-chunk size-retrieval depth combinations on the training set and selected eight optimized configurations for test-set evaluation. Combined with three prompts, these yielded 24 prompt-configuration combinations for comparison with ICD codes and the institutional PheNorm method. RAG achieved a mean sensitivity of 0.9019 (95% CI: 0.8866-0.9172), specificity of 0.7907 (0.7749-0.8066), PPV of 0.9405 (0.9365-0.9445), NPV of 0.6967 (0.6653-0.7281), and F1-score of 0.9204 (0.9124-0.9283). All combinations achieved higher PPV than ICD codes (0.7838). Compared with PheNorm, sensitivity was significantly higher (Holm-adjusted p < 0.001), while specificity differences were not significant. Paired bootstrap analyses showed higher NPV and F1-score, with no significant PPV difference. General-purpose embeddings showed higher sensitivity, whereas biomedical embeddings exhibited higher specificity and PPV. Few-shot prompting increased specificity and PPV but reduced sensitivity. Token usage varied substantially across embedding models. These findings suggest the importance of aligning RAG design with task-specific clinical priorities and token efficiency.

infographic.key_insight: RAG-based type 2 diabetes phenotyping achieved a mean F1-score of 0.9204, with embedding and prompt choices shifting sensitivity, specificity, and token use.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Configurable RAG may support EHR-based research cohort identification, but performance priorities must be matched to the phenotyping task.
method: Processed 170,678 clinical notes from 275 ICD-screened patients using GPT-4o.
Benchmarked seven embedding models and 350 embedding–chunk size–retrieval depth combinations on training data.
Evaluated eight optimized configurations with three prompts against ICD codes and PheNorm.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 24 test-set prompt–configuration combinations, mean sensitivity was 0.9019 and specificity was 0.7907; all combinations exceeded ICD-code PPV, and sensitivity significantly exceeded PheNorm.
infographic.watch_item: Findings from a small, ICD-screened cohort may not generalize to unselected populations or other conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Systematic Benchmarking and Optimization of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for Clinical Phenotyping: A Type II Diabetes Case Study in an ICD-Screened Cohort

title: Automating postmarketing pharmacovigilance with large language model agents
authors: Zhang, R.; Zhou, Y.; Chui, C. S. L.; Yu, D.; Wu, Z.; Luo, R.
abstract: Postmarketing pharmacovigilance relies on spontaneous adverse event reporting and labor-intensive observational studies, which suffer from underreporting and delayed risk detection. Large language model (LLM) agents could automate real-world evidence generation, but generalist agents make ad hoc analytical decisions that compromise epidemiological validity and reproducibility. Here we present MedCheckpoint, a multi-agent LLM system for automated postmarketing pharmacovigilance. MedCheckpoint grounds each analytical stage in a curated, source-traceable medical knowledge base, locks core study-design parameters before execution, performs patient-level analyses with human-written deterministic statistical tools, and enforces checkpoint rules that abort infeasible analyses, with optional human-in-the-loop review. We evaluated MedCheckpoint using a 54-question benchmark on a dual-purpose simulated electronic health record (EHR) testbed of 2.7 million individuals, designed with reliable clinical signals to evaluate routine analytical accuracy alongside spurious signals to stress-test system rigor. Across the benchmark, MedCheckpoint outperformed two coding-agent baselines in report quality across five dimensions rated by three independent LLM judges (overall means 4.81-4.88 versus 4.25-4.55 and 4.02-4.29) and yielded higher run-to-run consistency (mean within-question standard deviation 0.116-0.186 versus up to 0.440). Crucially, while baselines failed on up to 2 of 21 runs when handling infeasible comparisons or unmeasurable outcomes, MedCheckpoint produced no misleading failures across all seven stress-test trap questions with known data limitations. MedCheckpoint enables reliable, auditable, and scalable pharmacovigilance analysis.

infographic.key_insight: MedCheckpoint uses knowledge-grounded agents, locked study designs, and deterministic statistical tools to make automated drug-safety analyses more consistent and auditable.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The system could support postmarketing drug-safety research, but its performance on real-world clinical data remains unestablished.
method: Ground analytical stages in a curated, source-traceable medical knowledge base.
Lock core study-design parameters and analyze patient-level data with human-written statistical tools.
Abort infeasible analyses through checkpoints, with optional human review.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 54 questions using simulated EHRs for 2.7 million individuals, MedCheckpoint outperformed two coding-agent baselines in LLM-rated report quality and consistency, with no misleading failures across seven stress-test trap questions.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation relied on simulated EHRs and LLM judges; real-world validation and independent expert assessment are needed.
infographic.paper_title: Automating postmarketing pharmacovigilance with large language model agents

title: Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST): Comparing Self-Triage Systems and Multiple Generations of OpenAI Models Against Preliminary Expert Consensus
authors: Kroll, L. E.; Seidel, A.; Schuster, J.; Steiger, E.; Schoepke, T.; von Stillfried, D.; BeST Study Group,
abstract: As digital self-triage becomes more widely used, quality assurance requires evaluation of both emergency recognition and overall agreement with clinical judgement, including how these outcomes differ across generations of large language models. The Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST) project intends to provide a framework to compare systems for digital self-triage against a medical gold standard in Germany. As a first step in developing and demonstrating the methodology, we compared study-specific implementations of SmED 5.4.11 accessed via API and Infermedica Engine API via Microsoft Azure Healthcare Agent Service with five structured OpenAI configurations spanning multiple model generations: gpt-4.1, gpt-5.4, gpt-5.6-luna, gpt-5.6-sol, and gpt-6-astra. The manufacturers of SmED and Infermedica offer MDR-certified Class IIb triage products, but these certified products were not directly evaluated. An LLM-based patient actor covered 480 physician-curated vignettes derived from German routine triage data. A pool of seven physicians provided preliminary reference classifications and consensus for 480 vignettes. Recommendations were mapped to three urgency categories-emergency, acute, and not urgent-and evaluated using winsorised weights derived from routine triage frequencies. Weighted emergency sensitivity ranged from 51.3% (95% CI 35.566.3%) for gpt-4.1 to 99.9% (99.7-100.0%) for gpt-6-astra. Weighted exact three-category agreement (accuracy) ranged from 54.4% to 68.8%; gpt-4.1 achieved the highest agreement despite the lowest emergency sensitivity. No system performed best across all urgency categories. The later-generation OpenAI configurations showed a more precautionary triage profile resembling SmED, with higher sensitivity for emergency cases; gpt-6-astra showed the strongest shift. This cross-sectional comparison across model generations suggests a shift towards more precautionary triage behaviour, without establishing a longitudinal improvement in accuracy. These findings highlight the limitations of overall agreement for evaluating self-triage and support category-specific assessment. Broader expert consensus and evaluation, as well as further steps to reduce dependence on SmED-derived source data, are needed and planned before drawing conclusions about clinical safety.

infographic.key_insight: Later-generation OpenAI configurations showed higher emergency sensitivity, but no system performed best across all urgency categories.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Self-triage evaluation should assess emergency recognition separately from overall agreement, because high agreement can coexist with missed emergencies.
method: Compared study-specific SmED and Infermedica implementations with five structured OpenAI configurations.
Used an LLM-based patient actor across 480 physician-curated vignettes derived from German routine triage data.
Compared three-category urgency recommendations with preliminary physician consensus using frequency-based weights.
infographic.evidence_signal: Weighted emergency sensitivity ranged from 51.3% to 99.9%, while exact three-category agreement ranged from 54.4% to 68.8%; gpt-4.1 had the highest agreement but lowest emergency sensitivity.
infographic.watch_item: This vignette-based, cross-sectional comparison used preliminary expert consensus and did not directly evaluate the manufacturers’ certified triage products or establish longitudinal accuracy improvement.
infographic.paper_title: Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST): Comparing Self-Triage Systems and Multiple Generations of OpenAI Models Against Preliminary Expert Consensus

title: Generative AI Versus Primary Care Physicians from Plan Initiation to Long-Term Maintenance of Chronic Disease Self-Management: A Vignette-Based Validation Study
authors: Zhao, Z.; Yang, H.; Wang, Q.; Wang, Y.; Cheng, W.; Ma, X.
abstract: BackgroundGenerative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may provide personalised and dynamically adjustable support for chronic disease self-management. However, previous studies have largely focused on isolated questions and a limited range of evaluation dimensions. ObjectiveTo compare the quality of self-management advice generated by GenAI and primary care physicians (PCPs) across multiple stages of chronic disease management and evaluation dimensions. MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional, source-blinded comparative evaluation using 15 standardised vignettes of diabetes and hypertension derived from authentic primary care follow-up records. Each vignette comprised three sequential management stages, with medical accuracy, readability, and behaviour-change potential assessed across the three simulated stages; individualisation and multidisciplinary integration at plan initiation; contextual adaptability during acute adjustment; and empathy during long-term maintenance. The GenAI system and 22 PCPs independently generated advice which was independently rated by three clinicians, one each from general practice, endocrinology, and cardiology. across seven dimensions. Linear mixed-effects models were used for the primary comparisons, and case-level paired and physician-distribution analyses were conducted as robustness analyses. ResultsThe GenAI system achieved estimated marginal means above 4.0 in all dimensions except readability. It scored significantly higher than PCPs in six of the seven dimensions, with adjusted mean differences ranging from 1.16 to 1.56 points (P<.001). Readability was the only exception, with no significant difference between GenAI and PCPs (-0.22, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.11; P=.19). The GenAI mean exceeded the individual means of all recruited PCPs in the six dimensions but ranked at approximately the 23rd percentile for readability. ConclusionsOur findings indicated the GenAI system may generate more highly rated self-management advice than PCPs across most evaluated dimensions but offered no advantage in readability. These findings provide pre-implementation evidence for GenAI as a potential source of structured and adaptive chronic disease self-management support. Patient-level pilot studies and subsequent randomised trials are needed to determine its acceptability and effects on behaviour and clinical outcomes.

infographic.key_insight: GenAI self-management advice outscored primary care physicians in six of seven rated dimensions, but not readability.
infographic.clinical_relevance: GenAI may support structured diabetes and hypertension self-management advice, though benefits for patients remain untested.
method: Source-blinded comparison using 15 standardised diabetes and hypertension vignettes.
One GenAI system and 22 primary care physicians generated advice across three simulated management stages.
Three clinicians rated seven dimensions; primary comparisons used linear mixed-effects models.
infographic.evidence_signal: GenAI’s adjusted score advantages ranged from 1.16 to 1.56 points across six dimensions (P<.001); readability showed no significant difference.
infographic.watch_item: This vignette-based evaluation assessed advice quality, not real-world safety, patient understanding, or long-term health outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: Generative AI Versus Primary Care Physicians from Plan Initiation to Long-Term Maintenance of Chronic Disease Self-Management: A Vignette-Based Validation Study

title: MENTOR: An Evidence-Informed Large Language Model-Based Multi-Agent System for Efficient Selection of Institution-Specific Negative Control Outcomes
authors: Yang, T.; Chang, J.; Kim, Y.; Cho, J.; Choi, K.; Son, M.; Kim, C.
abstract: ObjectiveNegative control outcomes (NCOs) help detect and correct systematic error in observational studies, yet their selection remains largely manual. The Common Evidence Model (CEM) can generate candidate lists, but researchers must still screen them for plausibility as true nulls and for sufficient observation in each institutions data. We developed and evaluated MENTOR (Multi-agent Evidence-informed Negative conTrol Outcome selection with Reasoning), a multi-agent system of large language models (LLMs) that combines CEM evidence with LLM reasoning to select institution-specific NCOs. MethodsFour LLM agents operate on an institutions Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership common data model. A Curator summarizes drug labels, a Suggester assesses locally frequent candidates with CEM evidence and a first-pass LLM judgment, an Adjudicator resolves their disagreements, and a Diagnostician relaxes the patient-count threshold until a target number of NCOs is met. Using Qwen3.6-27B, we evaluated 349 candidates for three drug pairs in a Korean tertiary hospitals electronic health records (2.9 million patients) against a blinded LLM judge from a different model family, validated by three experts on 90 candidates. We compared accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV), and sensitivity with CEM-only and first-pass-LLM-only selection. ResultsMENTOR proposed 243 NCOs versus 121 by CEM-only, with higher accuracy (0.83 [0.79-0.87] vs. 0.53 [0.48-0.58]), sensitivity (0.89 vs. 0.41), and PPV (0.86 vs. 0.79). Judge-expert agreement was {kappa}=0.63. Adjudication, needed for 44.1% of candidates, added little accuracy, and only with reasoning mode. Concordant acceptances, which bypass it, contained about half of the false positives. Only 7%-9% of CEM-proposed outcomes had at least 10,000 patients at the institution. ConclusionCombining LLM judgments with CEM evidence and local data yielded more NCOs, with higher PPV, than CEM alone. Restricting reasoning to discordant candidates kept computation time below 40% of that with reasoning in all agents. Every decision comes with its evidence and rationale for investigators final review.

infographic.key_insight: MENTOR combined LLM reasoning, evidence, and local patient counts to select more negative control outcomes with higher accuracy and positive predictive value than evidence-only selection.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The system could streamline selection of institution-specific negative control outcomes used to assess systematic error in observational studies, while retaining investigator review.
method: Four LLM agents summarize drug labels, screen candidates, resolve disagreements, and adjust patient-count thresholds.
Combines Common Evidence Model evidence with institution-specific OMOP data.
Limits reasoning to disputed candidates, using less than 40% of the computation time required for reasoning in all agents.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 349 candidates for three drug pairs at one Korean hospital with 2.9 million patients, MENTOR selected 243 outcomes versus 121 with CEM alone, achieving accuracy of 0.83 versus 0.53 against a blinded LLM judge validated by three experts on 90 candidates.
infographic.watch_item: Single-site evaluation and reliance on an LLM reference judge limit certainty; accepted outcomes still require investigator review.
infographic.paper_title: MENTOR: An Evidence-Informed Large Language Model-Based Multi-Agent System for Efficient Selection of Institution-Specific Negative Control Outcomes

title: Ontology-Based SEA-CDM Integration for Vaccine Clinical Trials: Query, Similarity, and Design Recommendation
authors: Zhu, J.; Yeh, F.-Y.; Zheng, J.; He, Y.
abstract: ClinicalTrials.gov provides valuable information for vaccine research, but fragmented data structures and inconsistent vaccine naming complicate systematic cross-trial analysis. The Study-Experiment-Assay Common Data Model (SEA-CDM) provides a standardized structure for biomedical study data, while biomedical ontologies supply semantic relationships among concepts. We extracted 9,147 vaccine-related study records from the Aggregate Analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov (AACT) database, mapped their records into SEA-CDM, and linked vaccine products and reported adverse events (AEs) to the Vaccine Ontology (VO) and Ontology of Adverse Events (OAE), respectively. Building on the existing Ontology-based SEA Network (OSEAN), we organized the integrated data into relational tables and a Neo4j knowledge graph while retaining links to original registrations. We evaluated three applications to assess semantic trial retrieval, context-aware AE ranking and trial similarity, and trial design recommendation. First, VO-based query expansion retrieved 41 candidate RNA vaccine trials compared with 16 using exact VO identifier matching. Second, a context-aware AE ranking model incorporating SEA-CDM features and VO-derived vaccine families improved recall@10 from 0.317 to 0.383 over a frequency-based baseline. TransE and CompGCN embeddings achieved Hits@10 of 0.950 and 0.946, respectively, for retrieving trials sharing the same VO identifier within disease-specific candidate sets. Third, an ontology-based clinical trial design recommendation model was developed using several machine learning methods under leave-one-Material-out evaluation across 23 vaccine classes, although performance varied across classes. These findings demonstrate how structural and semantic integration can support multiple clinical trial analyses using vaccine studies as a case study. This framework provides a foundation for extending ontology-supported data integration and analysis to other clinical research domains.

infographic.key_insight: Integrating vaccine trial records with a common data model and biomedical ontologies improved semantic retrieval and adverse-event ranking while supporting trial similarity analysis and design recommendations.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could help researchers compare registered vaccine studies and inform trial planning, but it does not establish clinical safety or efficacy.
method: Mapped 9,147 AACT vaccine study records into SEA-CDM and linked vaccines and adverse events to VO and OAE.
Organized integrated records in relational tables and a Neo4j knowledge graph with links to original registrations.
Evaluated ontology-expanded search, adverse-event ranking, embedding-based trial similarity, and trial design recommendation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Ontology-expanded search retrieved 41 candidate RNA vaccine trials versus 16 with exact matching; adverse-event recall@10 rose from 0.317 to 0.383, and trial-similarity Hits@10 reached 0.950.
infographic.watch_item: Trial design recommendation performance varied across 23 vaccine classes under leave-one-Material-out evaluation, warranting further validation before use in trial planning.
infographic.paper_title: Ontology-Based SEA-CDM Integration for Vaccine Clinical Trials: Query, Similarity, and Design Recommendation

title: Sleep Variability From Routine Nursing Observation and Wearable Actigraphy and Post-Enrollment Length of Stay in Acute Psychiatric Inpatients: Prospective Observational Study
authors: Chen, H.-M.; Chen, Y.-L.; Yang, C. C.-H.
abstract: BackgroundLength of stay (LOS) in acute psychiatric inpatient settings is clinically and operationally important, but practical early markers for identifying patients at risk for prolonged hospitalization remain limited. ObjectiveTo evaluate whether sleep instability measured during the early inpatient observation period was associated with prolonged post-enrollment hospitalization in acute psychiatric inpatients. MethodsThis observational study included 94 consecutive patients admitted to an acute psychiatric inpatient unit. Monitoring began after study enrollment, and participants contributed 5 to 7 available nightly observations from wrist actigraphy and routine nursing observation; observations were not required to occur on consecutive calendar days. The primary exposure was intraindividual sleep variability (IISV), defined as the within-subject standard deviation of nightly total sleep time across available post-enrollment observations. The primary outcome was prolonged post-enrollment length of stay, defined using the 75th percentile of the cohort distribution. Age- and sex-adjusted logistic regression models evaluated associations, discrimination, calibration, and risk stratification. Total length of stay from admission was examined as a temporally distinct sensitivity estimand. ResultsParticipants were enrolled a median of 4 days after admission (IQR 2-7) and contributed 5 to 7 available nightly observations, which accumulated over a median of 8 calendar days (IQR 7-10); 39 of 94 observation series (41.5%) fell on consecutive calendar days. Prolonged post-enrollment hospitalization was defined as more than 24.0 days, yielding 23 events among 94 participants. Greater actigraphy-derived IISV was associated with prolonged post-enrollment hospitalization (adjusted odds ratio [OR], 2.30 per 1-hour increase; 95% CI, 1.08-4.93; P=.03), with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.756 (95% CI, 0.626-0.852; optimism-corrected, 0.725) compared with 0.692 for a model containing age and sex alone. Nursing-derived IISV showed an association of similar direction (adjusted OR, 3.10; 95% CI, 1.15-8.39; P=.03; AUC, 0.723; 95% CI, 0.571-0.837; optimism-corrected, 0.690). A combined model containing both measures did not improve discrimination over actigraphy alone (AUC, 0.751). ConclusionsSleep instability measured during the early inpatient observation period, derived independently from wearable actigraphy and from routine nursing sleep documentation, was associated with prolonged post-enrollment hospitalization. Because the outcome interval overlaps the period during which the sleep observations were accumulated, these findings describe an association across the early inpatient course rather than a prediction made at enrollment. The results support further evaluation of repeated sleep variability as a longitudinal inpatient measure; the variable observation schedule, single-center sample, and absence of external validation mean that clinical implementation remains premature.

infographic.key_insight: Greater night-to-night sleep variability was associated with prolonged post-enrollment hospitalization in acute psychiatric inpatients.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Sleep variability from wearable actigraphy or routine nursing observations may offer a practical marker for studying prolonged inpatient stays.
method: Prospective observational study of 94 acute psychiatric inpatients.
Sleep variability measured as each patient's standard deviation of nightly total sleep time across 5–7 available observations.
Age- and sex-adjusted logistic regression assessed post-enrollment stays exceeding 24 days.
infographic.evidence_signal: There were 23 prolonged-stay events; actigraphy-derived variability had an adjusted OR of 2.30 per additional hour (95% CI 1.08–4.93), with model AUC 0.756 versus 0.692 for age and sex alone.
infographic.watch_item: This small observational cohort establishes association, not causation or clinical readiness; observations were often nonconsecutive and began after enrollment rather than admission.
infographic.paper_title: Sleep Variability From Routine Nursing Observation and Wearable Actigraphy and Post-Enrollment Length of Stay in Acute Psychiatric Inpatients: Prospective Observational Study

title: DxToniaNet: A Neural Network for Estimating the Severity of Leg Dystonia in Children with Cerebral Palsy
authors: Bajpai, R.; Rust, A.; Lott, E.; Kim, S.; Gandham, S.; Chintalapati, K.; Blackburn, J.; Gelineau-Morel, R.; Kruer, M. C.; Mingbunjerdsuk, D.; O'Malley, J.; Tochen, L.; Waugh, J. L.; Wu, S.; Feyma, T.; Perlmutter, J. S.; Aravamuthan, B. R.
abstract: ImportanceLeg dystonia affects 50-80% of children with cerebral palsy (CP), but severity assessment remains subjective and time-consuming. Objective tools are urgently needed to quantify leg dystonia severity in clinical care and clinical trials. ObjectiveTo develop and validate a deep neural network (DxToniaNet) for leg dystonia severity estimation using 2D clinical video recordings. Design, Setting, and ParticipantsWe retrospectively analyzed video recordings of 298 children with cerebral palsy undergoing a seated hand open-close task as part of routine clinical care (Center 1: 193 videos, 720p/30fps; Center 2: 105 videos, 4K/60fps). Videos were rated for leg dystonia severity by a group of 7 experts using the Global Dystonia Rating Scale (GDRS) leg subscore (range 0-40) which has a minimum clinically important difference (MCID) of 4 points. Videos displaying leg dystonia (median expert GDRS score [≥]1) were used to develop and test a machine learning model (DxToniaNet) for estimating leg dystonia severity. Open-source software (OpenPose) estimated bilateral knee, ankle, and toe coordinates, normalized for height and camera positioning, and 69 variance and amplitude features were calculated based on established expert-cited features of leg dystonia. A neural network, DxToniaNet, was developed, trained and validated using 5-fold cross-validation on Center 1 videos before final testing on independent Center 2 videos. Main Outcome(s) and Measure(s){square}Mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), and accuracy in differentiating between videos with clinically meaningful differences in GDRS scores were calculated relative to experts median GDRS scores. ResultsWhen estimating experts leg GDRS scores in testing data, the proposed machine learning (ML) model yielded a MAE of 1.71 {+/-} 1.68 and RMSE of 2.21 {+/-} 0.34 (significantly less than the GDRS MCID of 4), and 90-94% accuracy in differentiating between videos with greater than a 4-point difference in the GDRS. Conclusions and RelevanceWe have demonstrated that DxToniaNet can accurately estimate leg dystonia severity compared to experts assessments with a small (clinically insignificant) error margin. Our methodology supports generalizability since DxToniaNet was developed and tested using independent videos datasets from different centers, recorded under different conditions. In the future, DxToniaNet may help facilitate standardized leg dystonia severity estimation in clinical care and clinical trials. Key pointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSCan a deep learning model use clinically-acquired videos to accurately estimate experts leg dystonia severity assessments in children with cerebral palsy? FindingsAn automated deep learning model (DxToniaNet) trained and tested on clinically-acquired smartphone videos of 298 children with cerebral palsy estimates leg dystonia severity with 90-94% accuracy compared to experts assessments. MeaningDxToniaNet is an objective and free tool to estimate leg dystonia severity and may thus help facilitate standardized tracking of longitudinal treatment responses and clinical trial outcomes.

infographic.key_insight: DxToniaNet estimated expert-rated leg dystonia severity from clinical videos of children with cerebral palsy, with a reported mean absolute error of 1.71 points on a 0–40 scale.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Video-based severity estimation could support more consistent assessments in clinical care and trials, but clinical utility requires further validation.
method: Used OpenPose to track bilateral knee, ankle, and toe coordinates during a seated hand open-close task.
Calculated 69 normalized movement variance and amplitude features.
Trained a neural network using five-fold cross-validation at Center 1, then tested it independently at Center 2.
infographic.evidence_signal: The retrospective study analyzed videos from 298 children across two centers; among videos showing dystonia, reported estimation error was below the 4-point clinically important difference, with 90–94% accuracy distinguishing videos whose expert scores differed by more than 4 points.
infographic.watch_item: Model development and testing included only videos showing dystonia, so performance for detecting its absence or across other tasks and settings remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: DxToniaNet: A Neural Network for Estimating the Severity of Leg Dystonia in Children with Cerebral Palsy

title: AToP: An Explainability Framework for Transformer-Based EHR Predictions Using Attribution-Guided Temporal Pattern Mining
authors: Belouali, A.; Kharrazi, H.
abstract: ObjectiveTo develop and evaluate AToP (Attribution to Temporal Patterns), a post-hoc explainability framework that converts per-token Integrated Gradients (IG) from a Transformer into structured temporal pattern narratives. Materials and MethodsAToP was applied to a single-stream Transformer trained on MIMIC-IV v3.1 (218,196 patients; 12.6% unplanned 30-day readmission). It mines frequent episodes from salient-token subsequences in the training cohort, aggregates attribution among patients whose records contain each token or pattern, and collapses near-duplicates by patient overlap. Validation used masking, reversed-order analysis, token-level faithfulness tests, and KernelSHAP comparison. ResultsThe Transformer achieved AUROC 0.77 and PR-AUC 0.34. Population-weighted attribution emphasized high-prevalence codes with small per-patient impact. Carrier-conditional attribution, the mean among patients with the token, surfaced rare high-attribution psychiatric markers including psychosis, self-harm overdose, suicidal ideation (SI), and severe major depressive disorder (MDD). Pattern-level attribution identified within-visit co-occurrences and cross-visit trajectories not captured by token rankings. Risk-increasing patterns included psychiatric sequences ({MDD, SI} [->] SI) and oncologic progressions (cancer anemia [->] ascites). Obstetric and chest pain evaluation patterns were associated with lower predicted readmission. DiscussionThe framework provides two complementary views of model predictions: carrier-conditional aggregation highlights rare, highly attributed clinical features, while temporal pattern analysis identifies within-visit combinations and cross-visit trajectories missed by token-level rankings. Masking and visit-order reversal provided evidence of correspondence with model behavior, but pattern attributions do not represent unique effects or establish clinical validity. ConclusionAToP turns a Transformers attributions into visit-anchored temporal pattern narratives, showing which events, in which order, contribute to its readmission predictions.

infographic.key_insight: AToP converts Transformer attributions into visit-anchored temporal patterns, revealing combinations and sequences missed by individual-code rankings.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework helps researchers interpret EHR-based readmission predictions without establishing that highlighted patterns are clinically valid risk factors.
method: Compute per-token Integrated Gradients for a Transformer predicting unplanned 30-day readmission.
Mine frequent temporal patterns from salient tokens and merge near-duplicates by patient overlap.
Compare population-weighted attribution with attribution averaged among patients carrying each token or pattern.
infographic.evidence_signal: On MIMIC-IV v3.1 data from 218,196 patients, the Transformer achieved AUROC 0.77 and PR-AUC 0.34; explanations were evaluated using masking, visit-order reversal, token-level faithfulness tests, and KernelSHAP comparison.
infographic.watch_item: Pattern attributions reflect model behavior, not unique causal effects or established clinical validity.
infographic.paper_title: AToP: An Explainability Framework for Transformer-Based EHR Predictions Using Attribution-Guided Temporal Pattern Mining

title: Silent Drift and Site-level Variance in Clinical AI: Real-world performance and subgroup analysis for post-market monitoring of an FDA-cleared artificial intelligence (AI) triage tool for high-risk use case of pulmonary embolism
authors: Dayma, K.; Newton, C.; Kawzowicz, M.; Patel, P.; Curl, R.; Ogden, K.
abstract: BackgroundFDA-cleared artificial intelligence (AI) triage tool for pulmonary embolism (PE) detection has been widely used; however, its performance has not been analyzed for subgroups, clinical sites, and temporal stability. MethodsThis retrospective, six-site health system study evaluated the Aidoc BriefCase PE triage model (K190072) across 14,736 CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) examinations between July 2023 and March 2026. Reference-standard PE characteristic labels were extracted from radiology reports using a zero-shot LLM pipeline validated against a radiologist-annotated 600 reports ({kappa} =0.98). Model performance was evaluated across demographics, embolus characteristics, and site. Temporal behavior was evaluated on operating point by logistic regression, with and without site adjustment, and by segmented regression. ResultsPE was present in 1,402/14,736 examinations (9.5%). Overall sensitivity was 64.1% (95% CI, 61.5-66.6%), specificity 98.8% (95% CI, 98.6-99.0%), compared with 93% sensitivity and 93.7% specificity in the FDA 510(k) summary. Sensitivity fell with peripherality (central 88.6%, lobar or segmental 63.1%, subsegmental 33.3%) and with chronicity (acute 65.5%, chronic 57.4%). Sensitivity differed significantly between the two highest-volume sites, 68.7% and 55.7% (P < .001), with CT scanner as the only variable different between the two sites. The false-positive rate fell 40% per year (P<.001) at a similar rate at two sites, while sensitivity fell 15% per year at site A (P<.036), from 72.5% to 65.0% between two halves of the study period. The manufacturer did not report model updates or threshold changes during the study period. ConclusionsDeployed sensitivity was substantially below the cleared benchmark and varied 13 points by site. The gradual shift in high specificity at the cost of low sensitivity, either from data drift or threshold change, either not monitored or not documented by the manufacturer, highlights the importance of independent continuous post-market monitoring.

infographic.key_insight: Real-world sensitivity of an FDA-cleared pulmonary embolism triage AI was 64.1%, versus 93% in its clearance summary, and varied by site and embolus location.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Lower detection sensitivity, particularly for peripheral emboli, underscores the importance of local validation and ongoing monitoring of AI triage tools.
method: Retrospective evaluation of 14,736 CT pulmonary angiography examinations across six sites, July 2023–March 2026.
Report-derived reference labels used an LLM pipeline validated against 600 radiologist-annotated reports (κ = 0.98).
Assessed performance across demographic and embolus subgroups, sites, and time.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 1,402 PE-positive examinations, overall sensitivity was 64.1% and specificity 98.8%; sensitivity was 68.7% versus 55.7% at the two highest-volume sites.
infographic.watch_item: Retrospective, report-based evaluation cannot establish whether temporal changes arose from data drift, undocumented threshold changes, or other factors.
infographic.paper_title: Silent Drift and Site-level Variance in Clinical AI: Real-world performance and subgroup analysis for post-market monitoring of an FDA-cleared artificial intelligence (AI) triage tool for high-risk use case of pulmonary embolism

title: Cytokine Signatures of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Myocarditis and the Modifying Role of Clonal Hematopoiesis: A Machine-Learning and Multi-Omics Study
authors: Manchanda, N.; Chehayeb, R. J.; Hong, D.; Jeyashanmugaraja, A.; Singh, J.; Cross, J. L.; Vijayram, A.; Martinez, C. M.; Jayakrishnan, R.; Christofides, A.; Lin, D.; Im, Y.; VanOudenhove, J.; Biancon, G.; Ibrahim, E.; Ardasheva, A.; Lin, E. Y. S.; Levine, R.; Cheng, E.; Halene, S.; Hwa, J.; Smith, N.; Villani, C.; Zhu, H.; Jha, A.; Kwan, J. M.
abstract: BackgroundImmune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) myocarditis affects up to 2% of patients on ICI and has up to a 50% mortality. Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) is a risk factor for ICI myocarditis. ObjectivesTo leverage a multi-omics approach to evaluate cytokines associated with ICI myocarditis, immunosuppression resistance, CHIP in ICI myocarditis and implicated pathways and cell type contributions. Methods236 cardio-oncology patients were enrolled, including 88 who were on ICI. Cytokine profiling from patients on ICI were sampled and analyzed using machine learning and explainable artificial intelligence. Single-cell multi-omics of peripheral blood from Yale (n=19), Stanford (n=25), and MGH (n=63) evaluated cell-type contributions of cytokines and implicated pathways. Validation of Yale proteomic analyses was done using the Stanford CYTOF dataset. ResultsTop features associated with ICI myocarditis included IL13, CXCL10, PDGF-A, CCL13, CCL17 and KITlg. Top KEGG pathways associated with ICI myocarditis and immunosuppression resistant ICI myocarditis included JAK-STAT signaling, IL17 signaling and lipid/atherosclerosis pathways. At the single-cell level, the consensus signals distinguishing myocarditis from non-myocarditis across cohorts was predominantly driven by module-level JAK-STAT, T-cell, and Toll-like receptor activation. Similar transcription gene programs were activated in CHIP carriers including modules implicated in the pro-inflammatory immune response, such as NF-kappa B, IL17, MAPK, and TNF pathways within CHIP cells spanning lymphoid (cytotoxic CD8+ NKT, and natural killer cells) and myeloid lineages. ConclusionsAcross cohorts, JAK-STAT signaling emerges as a convergent and potentially actionable axis in ICI myocarditis that is further amplified in CHIP carriers, supporting cytokine-guided risk stratification and JAK-STAT-directed immunosuppression as testable strategies.

infographic.key_insight: Machine learning and multi-omics identified cytokine signatures associated with ICI myocarditis, with JAK-STAT signaling emerging across cohorts and showing amplification in CHIP carriers.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These findings nominate cytokine-based risk assessment and JAK-STAT-targeted treatment as research strategies, not established clinical tools.
method: Machine learning and explainable AI analyzed cytokine profiles from ICI-treated patients.
Single-cell multi-omics mapped immune-cell contributions and inflammatory pathways across three cohorts.
Stanford CyTOF data validated Yale proteomic analyses.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study enrolled 236 cardio-oncology patients, including 88 receiving ICI, and analyzed single-cell cohorts from Yale (n=19), Stanford (n=25), and MGH (n=63).
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports associations but no predictive-performance metrics or treatment efficacy; clinical implementation requires prospective validation.
infographic.paper_title: Cytokine Signatures of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Myocarditis and the Modifying Role of Clonal Hematopoiesis: A Machine-Learning and Multi-Omics Study

title: Automatic classification of seizure adequacy in electroconvulsive therapy: A proof-of-concept study
authors: Panah, M.; Jessen, B. L.; Rand, A.; Jansen, T.; Jorgensen, M. B.; Morup, M.; Jorgensen, A.
abstract: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is the most effective treatment of a range of severe mental disorders and is annually given to more than a million patients worldwide. Dosing of the electrical charge is critical for efficacy and side-effect burden; however, it is currently based on manual assessment of seizure quality and exhibits substantial clinical heterogeneity. Here, we collected 1,000 ECT session electroencephalograms (EEG) from 130 individual ECT patients and made an expert-level classification of the EEGs into actionable seizure quality categories (null-response [0], threshold [T], and adequate [A]). We then trained a range of machine learning algorithms on the raw EEG data to classify the EEGs into these categories and tested for classification accuracy. The highest performing algorithm was able to classify the seizures with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curves of >0.9 for both the 0 vs. T and the T vs. A categories corresponding to excellent discrimination. In contrast, the accuracy of predicting seizure quality in subsequent treatments was only moderate. The addition of clinical variables to the models, such as demographics, anesthesia and anticonvulsant exposure, did not improve model performance. These results provide proof-of-concept of machine learning classification of seizure adequacy in ECT based on raw EEG data. The findings could pave the way for the development of more objective and personalized decision-support tools in ECT.

infographic.key_insight: Machine learning classified ECT seizure adequacy from raw EEG with ROC AUC above 0.9 for null-response versus threshold and threshold versus adequate seizures.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Automated EEG assessment could support more objective ECT dosing decisions, but improved treatment outcomes were not demonstrated.
method: Collected 1,000 ECT-session EEGs from 130 patients.
Assigned expert labels: null-response, threshold, or adequate.
Trained and evaluated multiple machine learning algorithms on raw EEG.
infographic.evidence_signal: The best model achieved ROC AUC above 0.9 for both reported category comparisons; adding clinical variables did not improve performance.
infographic.watch_item: Prediction of seizure quality in subsequent treatments was only moderate, limiting conclusions about prospective dosing support.
infographic.paper_title: Automatic classification of seizure adequacy in electroconvulsive therapy: A proof-of-concept study

title: Do Rule-Derived Labels Improve Prediction When Reported Labels Are Limited? A Two-Site Machine Learning Study
authors: SADI, T. H.; Ruthbah, C. A.
abstract: BackgroundRule-derived (weak) labels can enlarge a training set when reported labels are scarce. Their value depends on label quality, on how the extra records shift the training distribution, and on whether the comparison accounts for reported labels set aside for tuning or calibration. MethodsWe ran an exploratory label-budget experiment on Escherichia coli urine cultures from two de-identified electronic health record datasets: Stanford ARMD and UT Southwestern ARMD-UTSW. The task was to predict reported non-susceptibility to cefepime, cefoxitin and ceftazidime (Stanford) and to cefepime and ceftazidime (UT Southwestern). Reported-label budgets of 10%, 25%, 50% and 100% of development patients were drawn over five patient-disjoint outer splits. Logistic regression and histogram gradient boosting were trained with reported labels only, or with added rule-derived labels using equal weights, a tuning-selected weight, class-proportion adjustment or prior-probability correction. These were compared with an all-budget reported-only baseline that used every budgeted reported label for training. Stanford used the inferred labels released with the dataset and a feature set including resistance history. UT Southwestern used researcher-derived labels from Stanford rule text, which were not validated for that site, and an age-only primary model. Brier-score differences were assessed with paired patient-cluster bootstrap intervals. ResultsAll rule-derived labels were susceptible. Equal-weight augmentation lowered mean predicted risk well below observed prevalence (for example, Stanford cefepime at the 10% budget: 0.35% versus 4.85%) and had a higher Brier score than the all-budget baseline in every drug, model and budget summary. The tuning-selected weight did not consistently improve on the all-budget baseline. Its median Brier difference was positive in 38 of 40 drug, model and budget summaries. Its paired intervals lay above zero in 100 of 296 Stanford analyses and 31 of 198 UT Southwestern analyses, and below zero in 3 and 5. The tuning set often selected a weight of zero (146 of 296 and 153 of 198 analyses). At UT Southwestern, the age-only models showed little discrimination (median AUROC 0.49 to 0.54), so those comparisons mainly reflect calibration. ConclusionsUnder these designs, rule-derived labels did not consistently improve probability prediction over a reported-only model that used the whole reported-label budget for training. Evaluations of weak supervision should include such a baseline and should report calibration as well as discrimination.

infographic.key_insight: Adding rule-derived labels did not consistently improve prediction over using all budgeted reported labels, and equal weighting worsened Brier scores across all summarized settings.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Expanding antibiotic-resistance training data with rule-derived labels may underestimate non-susceptibility risk rather than improve predictions.
method: Studied E. coli urine cultures at Stanford and UT Southwestern using reported-label budgets of 10%, 25%, 50% and 100%.
Compared logistic regression and histogram gradient boosting with reported labels alone versus several rule-label augmentation strategies.
Evaluated five patient-disjoint outer splits using Brier scores and paired patient-cluster bootstrap intervals.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tuning-selected augmentation had worse median Brier scores than the all-budget reported-only baseline in 38 of 40 drug–model–budget summaries.
infographic.watch_item: All rule-derived labels were susceptible, and UT Southwestern's rules were not locally validated, limiting confidence in transportability.
infographic.paper_title: Do Rule-Derived Labels Improve Prediction When Reported Labels Are Limited? A Two-Site Machine Learning Study

title: LLM Representations Rival Traditional Predictors and Enhance Multimodal Prediction of APOE4 and Aβ-Burden
authors: Zadok, M.; Calderon, N.; Wald, Y.; Rein, N.; Ganmore, I.; Lesman-Segev, O.; Almog, G.; Shamir, T.; Ackler, R.; Leviner, S. Y.; Noimark, G.; Levy, G.; Mueller, K. D.; Ravona Springer, R.; Schnaider Beeri, M.; Reichart, R.
abstract: Spontaneous language offers a scalable, non-invasive approach for identifying biological indicators of preclinical Alzheimers disease (AD). We examined prediction of APOE4 carrier status and cerebral amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}) burden using Cookie Theft picture-descriptions from two cohorts, including Hebrew- and English-speakers (IRAP, N=134; and WRAP, N=1,541). A{beta} burden was classified across lowest-quartile, median, and highest-quartile cutoffs, capturing accumulation below conventional amyloid-positivity thresholds. We compared embeddings from pretrained large language models (LLMs) to standard cognitive test scores, reflecting current clinical assessment, and theory-driven linguistic features, reflecting traditional language analysis. Embedding-based models achieve the highest F1 among constituent models in five of eight tasks for APOE4 status and global A{beta}. High prediction disagreement suggests complementary signals between approaches. An any-positive ensemble significantly outperforms every constituent model and a prior-informed random baseline across all eight tasks, and is also significantly superior to all constituent models in 21 of 24 regional A{beta} tasks. These findings highlight the complementarity of LLM-based, theory-driven, and cognitive measures for predicting AD-related genetic risk and pathology, and supports development of early screening approaches.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-derived language representations complemented cognitive scores and traditional linguistic features, with combined models improving prediction of APOE4 carrier status and amyloid-β burden.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Picture-description language may support research toward non-invasive early risk screening, but these findings do not establish clinical diagnostic utility.
method: Analyzed Cookie Theft picture descriptions from Hebrew- and English-speaking cohorts.
Compared pretrained LLM embeddings with cognitive test scores and theory-driven linguistic features.
Combined predictions using an any-positive ensemble across APOE4 and amyloid-β classification tasks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across IRAP (N=134) and WRAP (N=1,541), LLM models achieved the highest constituent-model F1 in 5 of 8 APOE4/global amyloid-β tasks; the ensemble significantly outperformed all constituent models in all 8 tasks and 21 of 24 regional amyloid-β tasks.
infographic.watch_item: An any-positive ensemble may increase false positives; clinical use requires assessment of specificity, calibration, and external generalizability.
infographic.paper_title: LLM Representations Rival Traditional Predictors and Enhance Multimodal Prediction of APOE4 and Aβ-Burden

title: Enrollees and Early Lessons from an Agentic Healthcare Platform with Physicians in the Loop
authors: Shen, Z.; Ramachandran, A.; Hsiang, E.; Gill, J.; Miller, R.; Stark, N. R.
abstract: Agentic healthcare platforms that combine large language models with physician oversight are growing quickly, but little is known about who uses them. We characterized 3,223 enrollees of Lotus AI, a free, physician-supervised agentic platform, who completed onboarding, messaged the agent, and had a linked health record between February and July 2026, and compared them with national benchmarks. Median age was 51 years and 62% were male. Chronic condition prevalence exceeded 2024 National Health Interview Survey estimates in every age band by 4 to 7 percentage points; 18% had a functional or symptom-defined disorder; among the 30% with four or more ambulatory visits in the prior year, care was spread across nearly five providers, with 44% meeting a threshold for high fragmentation. Users with functional disorders generated 1.8 times as many physician escalations and 2.6 times as many laboratory orders as other users, but no more prescriptions. This profile differs from the younger, predominantly female populations reported for direct-to-consumer telemedicine. It moves chronic disease management, functional disorder pathways, and care coordination from aspirations to design requirements, and we argue that deployed AI care platforms should characterize their populations against national benchmarks early.

infographic.key_insight: Lotus AI enrollees had higher chronic condition prevalence than national benchmarks, highlighting chronic care and coordination needs in physician-supervised AI platforms.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The enrollee profile suggests these platforms should prioritize chronic disease management, functional disorder pathways, and coordination across providers.
method: Characterized 3,223 enrollees who completed onboarding, messaged the agent, and had linked health records during February–July 2026.
Compared demographics and chronic condition prevalence with national benchmarks.
Examined care fragmentation and service use among enrollees.
infographic.evidence_signal: Chronic condition prevalence exceeded 2024 NHIS estimates by 4–7 percentage points across age bands; enrollees with functional disorders had 1.8× as many physician escalations and 2.6× as many laboratory orders, but no more prescriptions.
infographic.watch_item: This selected, single-platform observational cohort does not establish clinical benefit, safety, or generalizability to other populations.
infographic.paper_title: Enrollees and Early Lessons from an Agentic Healthcare Platform with Physicians in the Loop

title: Detecting Contradictory Evidence on Drug-Disease Associations at Scale
authors: Lan, M.; Menke, J.; Liu, S.; Lu, Z.; Kilicoglu, H.
abstract: Contradictory claims about drug efficacy across randomized controlled trials (RCTs) complicate evidence-based medicine, yet existing automated methods classify isolated sentence pairs and do not explain why studies disagree. We present DrugCon, a large language model (LLM)-based framework that extracts study conclusions from RCT abstracts, links these claims when they concern the same drug-disease association, detects contradictions with counterfactual reasoning, and explains them using a taxonomy of ten study-level factors such as population, dosage, and outcome measures. Applying DrugCon to 224,756 RCT abstracts, we built DO_SCPLOWRUGC_SCPLOWCO_SCPLOWONC_SCPLOW-BO_SCPLOWENCHC_SCPLOW, an exhaustively annotated benchmark of 542 contradictory claim pairs from 819 abstracts. Most contradictions involve more than one study-level factor (75.5%). The most common are differences in outcome measures (64.0%), populations (51.3%), and dosage or exposure duration (35.6%). DrugCon achieves an F1 score of 0.744 for contradiction detection, outperforming rule-based, supervised, and natural language inference baselines, and an F1 of 0.482 for identifying explanatory study factors. DrugCon enables scalable and explainable analysis of contradictory clinical evidence.

infographic.key_insight: DrugCon detects contradictory trial conclusions about the same drug–disease association and identifies study-level differences that may explain the disagreement.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could support evidence review by highlighting conflicting efficacy claims and differences in trial populations, outcomes, or treatment exposure.
method: Uses an LLM to extract conclusions from randomized controlled trial abstracts and link claims about the same drug–disease association.
Applies counterfactual reasoning to detect contradictions.
Explains disagreements using a taxonomy of 10 study-level factors.
infographic.evidence_signal: From 224,756 RCT abstracts, researchers built an annotated benchmark of 542 contradictory claim pairs from 819 abstracts; DrugCon achieved F1 scores of 0.744 for contradiction detection and 0.482 for explanatory-factor identification.
infographic.watch_item: Abstract-only analysis may miss important trial details, and explanatory-factor identification remains imperfect; flagged disagreements require expert review.
infographic.paper_title: Detecting Contradictory Evidence on Drug-Disease Associations at Scale

title: Protocol and Statistical Analysis Plan for the Hyperangulated versus Standard Geometry Laryngoscope Blade (ANGLE) Trial
authors: DeMasi, S. C.; Semler, M. W.; Robinson, A. E.; White, H. D.; Buell, K. G.; Lyle, C.; Gottlieb, M.; Barnett, L. H.; Qadir, N.; Kloosterboer, A. L.; Resnick-Ault, D.; Gandotra, S.; Beach, L. L.; Vonderhaar, D. J.; Haas, T.; Barraza, M. J.; Gordon, A. J.; Landefeld, K. R.; Gibbs, K. W.; Brown, C. A.; Wilkerson, R. G.; Lim, S. C.; Khan, A.; Muhs, A. L.; Qiao, X.; Herbert, T.; Walker, J. E.; Brainard, J. C.; Douin, D. J.; Russell, D. W.; Ghamande, S. A.; Jackson, K. E.; Alcorn, T.; Alwood, S. M.; Kirincich, J.; Bartuska, A. P.; Bowery, E. K.; Sachs, N.; Whitson, M. R.; Brueder, A. P.; Martin, A. L.
abstract: BackgroundEmergency tracheal intubation is common and high risk. Although guidelines recommend using a video laryngoscope to intubate critically ill adults, whether a hyperangulated or standard-geometry blade is more likely to achieve successful intubation on the first attempt remains unknown. Research QuestionDoes the use of a video laryngoscope with a hyperangulated blade increase the incidence of successful intubation on the first attempt among adults undergoing emergency tracheal intubation, compared to use of a video laryngoscope with a standard-geometry blade? Study Design and MethodsThe HyperANgulated versus Standard Geometry Laryngoscope BladE (ANGLE) trial is a pragmatic, multicenter, unblinded, parallel-group, randomized trial being conducted in 28 sites (10 emergency departments and 18 intensive care units) in the United States. The trial compares use of a video laryngoscope with a hyperangulated blade versus a standard-geometry blade among 2,500 critically ill adults undergoing emergency tracheal intubation. The primary outcome is successful intubation on the first attempt. The secondary outcome is the incidence of hypoxemia during intubation. Enrollment began on December 30, 2025, and is expected to conclude in 2027. InterpretationThe ANGLE trial will provide important data on the effects of the use of a video laryngoscope with a hyperangulated blade versus standard-geometry blade on successful intubation on the first attempt and other outcomes of emergency tracheal intubation. Specifying the protocol and statistical analysis plan before the conclusion of enrollment increases the rigor, reproducibility, and transparency of the trial. Trial RegistryClinicalTrials.gov; No.: NCT07223762; URL: www.clinicaltrials.gov
primary_category: intensive care and critical care medicine
categories: intensive care and critical care medicine

infographic.key_insight: The ANGLE trial will test whether hyperangulated video laryngoscope blades improve first-attempt intubation success compared with standard-geometry blades.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The findings could inform blade selection for emergency tracheal intubation in critically ill adults.
method: Pragmatic, multicenter, unblinded, parallel-group randomized trial.
Planned enrollment of 2,500 adults across 10 emergency departments and 18 intensive care units in the United States.
Primary outcome: first-attempt intubation success; secondary outcome: hypoxemia during intubation.
infographic.evidence_signal: This protocol reports no comparative results; enrollment began December 30, 2025, and is expected to conclude in 2027.
infographic.watch_item: The unblinded design may allow operator expectations to influence performance; this is a device-comparison trial, not an AI study.

title: Artificial intelligence for pulmonary tuberculosis detection on chest X-ray images: A systematic review and diagnostic accuracy meta-analysis
authors: Mahfuz, S. A.; Al Mahfuz, S.; Roy, S. K.; Rahman, H. I.; Nahar, A.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based computer-aided detection (CAD) of tuberculosis (TB) on chest X-ray (CXR) may standardize screening and triage in settings with few radiologists but its accuracy in clinical cohorts remains uncertain. We searched five databases (PubMed, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, OpenAlex, Lens.org) on 15 March 2026 for studies published between January 2020 and March 2026, and we appraised these studies using QUADAS-2. Evaluations from clinical cohorts with complete 2 x 2 data and a microbiological or composite reference standard for all participants were pooled using a bivariate random-effects model, with 95% prediction intervals. We accounted for overlapping participants by performing a post hoc analysis with one evaluation per cohort and used GRADE to assess the certainty of the evidence. No protocol was prepared or registered. We included 21 studies (26 evaluations of AI models). Nine evaluations from three independent cohorts were pooled. Pooled sensitivity was 0.896 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.874 to 0.915, prediction interval 0.798 to 0.950) and pooled specificity was 0.689 (95% CI 0.642 to 0.732; prediction interval 0.499 to 0.831). Both confidence intervals include the World Health Organization (WHO) triage thresholds (sensitivity 90%, specificity 70%). When a screening study with partial verification was added, pooled specificity increased to 0.735. Eighteen of 24 assessed evaluations were at high risk of bias and only 1 of 21 studies was prospective, fully verified, externally validated and met the WHO thresholds. Certainty of evidence was low for sensitivity and very low for specificity. A subsequent PubMed search found additional eligible clinical evaluations that were not screened, so the review is incomplete for those studies. In clinical cohorts, AI-CXR sensitivity is close to the WHO triage target, and specificity is close to, but not clearly above, its target. The evidence is pooled across only three cohorts, and specificity varies by product and setting. Thresholds need to be calibrated locally, and prospective, externally validated evaluations are needed before widespread deployment.
